stem.en: Labrador lies further south than Norway, yet icebergs float off Labrador while the sea off Norway stays open. What explains the ice off Labrador?

text.en: The sea there is shallow, so ice lasts through summer.

feedback.en: Depth is not the reason. The ice forms because of the cold water that arrives along that coast.

text.en: A wind from Norway blows the ice across the ocean.

feedback.en: The ice does not come from Norway, whose sea stays largely free of ice. Look at the water along Canada's coast.

text.en: A current brings freezing water along that coast.

feedback.en: Yes. The Labrador Current flows along the east coast of Canada and carries freezing water.

text.en: Icebergs always gather at that one latitude.

feedback.en: Latitude does not decide it. Norway is further north and has less ice, so something else must be at work.

explanation.en: The Labrador Current is a cold current. It flows along the east coast of Canada and carries freezing water, so sea ice and icebergs form there even at a lower latitude. Latitude alone does not decide how cold a sea is.

hints.en: Ask where the water along that coast comes from.
